text: Good afternoon. I'd like to call the February 10th, 2026 School Board Budget Work Session to order. First, we have an annual report from the Citizens Budget Advisory Committee for Mrs. Patel. Hi, everyone. My name is Reynal Patel, and I am the chair for the CBAC Citizens Budget Advisory Committee this year.

With me, I have two members joining me, and collectively we will plan to provide our recommendations for FY27. I wanted to mention the purpose of the CBAC committee is to assist CCPS board in the evaluation and allocation of resources to ensure high-quality, effective, and efficient school division.

Here is a list of our current CBAC members, and I would like to take this opportunity to thank each and every one of them for their time, their insights, and providing their time to the CBAC committee. As you can see, our committee meets typically around 10 times a year.

And on top of that, we also have scheduled school visits that we do as well. Having said that, I'm going to pass it on to Lisa, and she's going to carry us forward to the next few slides here. Hi, I'm Lisa Mansfield.

In order to get a good look at where our money is allocated, we had a combination of resources at our disposal. We had presentations in many of our meetings from a variety of divisions across our school system. We also had many members of the school division available to provide input and context to these discussions, including but not limited to Dr. Murray, Bob Meister, and Ann Coker.

But I would argue that the most insight we received was from our on-site school visits. Each member of the committee was given the opportunity to tour two schools in their district, and while we were there, we were able to have meetings and discuss the needs with both administrators and instructional staff, and in some cases, current students.

The schools varied not only by grade level, we went to elementary, middle, and high school, but also by age, those new schools and the older ones that required more maintenance costs. And we also toured schools that were overcrowded and those that did not have any capacity needs. These visits provided a great deal of information to help us focus our attention on the needs within our schools.

Over the past few years, we have made substantial headway on key items this advisory committee has recognized, particularly regarding employee compensation and replacement cycles. However, we feel there is more work to be done, especially in these four areas, teacher compensation and hourly wages, vacancies and hard to staff positions, long term solutions for major maintenance funding and accelerating progress on capital projects, especially when we are looking to address overcrowding and inadequate facilities.

We will address these themes in the next few slides. the contractual obligation standpoint, as well as the health and dental insurance increases that are going to be starting in January 2027. I'm going to pass it on to Bill. He's going to talk about our ongoing unfunded themes here.

And I saw that firsthand with some of these school visits, you know, boots on the ground. Ongoing maintenance, I think you probably are tired of hearing about that. Or, you know, in the case of, say, a place like Providence Middle School, it was, boy, it would really be nice to have one more ESL teacher. So, like I said in the beginning, I'm not sure this is any surprise, but, you know, these are definitely things that keep percolating up for us.

We're also very fortunate in the fact that our rating as a county is so good for borrowing. And we do have, you know, a large number that could be borrowed. Of course, those decisions aren't going to be made by me, but that's a position that I'd rather be in than not be in.

But I'm sure you've considered that. And so I'll leave it to you, we're all here to close out for us, okay? Thank you, Bill. As we conclude our recommendations, wanted to share our excitement to see the 5% in the proposed budget as it brings us one step closer to our compensation goals.

I would like to also thank Dr. Murray, Mr. Meister, and his team for continuing to put the employee compensation on the front burner. Looking at the other unfunded themes, as you heard from our presentation, we would like to draw your attention to those unfunded ongoing themes and emphasize that most of those themes came from conversations we have had at the school visits.

And so kind of what Bill has mentioned, you know, feet on the ground and kind of having that information directly from the schools around CCPS. So our ask is to, again, emphasize and focus and see if we can accelerate some of the unfunded themes in a timely manner.
That's all we have today. We can take any of your questions. Excuse me. Thank you. Board members, is there any discussion? Ms. Cooker. Thank you. I just want to say thank you to the whole CBAC team.

You are very engaged in our meetings and ask really pointed questions. And thank you for your presentation here today. And, yes, it's good to hear from those that are out there in the schools and hearing their needs.

And thank you for your list of unfunded so we can look to those if more money falls from the sky. So thank you very much. Thank you. Mr. Bronto. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you very much as well to the CBAC committee.

Greatly appreciate the time and effort that you put into this. One of the things that you mentioned, which I was really pleased to hear, is that you're not just sitting in a room listening to presentations, which there's nothing wrong with that. You have a better understanding and a better feel for what's going on when you go and you visit our schools.

And so you took time out of your day to go and do that. And I greatly appreciate the commitment that you have to CCPS, to whether you use PTO or whatever you did to take away from your life and your job to come and help us understand better where we could potentially direct additional funds, more funds, future funds, what have you.

And listening to the teachers and to the principal and talking to those on site is, I think, invaluable. And I greatly appreciate that. And I do want to go down this path real quick. So we did have a join. There was three districts that met last night for their budget town hall.

And because there are three of us there, it was, you know, an announced meeting. And so I bring that up to say it was on record. And we had an individual that was present that had mentioned about disagreeing with the 5%. And it should really be 3.7% increase for our teachers.
Are you able to speak to why you believe the 5% is exactly where we need to be right now? I mean, I can speak for myself and others can certainly. Sure, go ahead. Thank you.

Yes, I was there and I heard what that individual said. I mean, I understand his point. You know, anytime that anybody raises taxes or, you know, any government entity needs more money, just remember it comes by force from your fellow citizens.

But then on the flip side, let me see if I can find the slide here. He's not looking at this. And honestly, I think this gentleman, well-intentioned, was pretty ignorant of the laws of supply and the laws of demand.

So when you look at this slide, Mr. Prender, that he was not privy to, maybe if we'd had that slide, it would have made a difference. Probably not, though, with this gentleman. But obviously, looking at that and knowing a little bit about the background, it's hard enough to get a math teacher. As a matter of fact, the principal in Providence Middle School said that they had, and I forget the term they used for it, it was kind of like the best you can do.

It was like you had some teacher in the room, and then on the video screen was a math teacher. I can remember back to calculus with Mr. Howe. I couldn't imagine not having him in that classroom. I wouldn't have learned a thing. It would have been very difficult. And there's a reason why I'm going down this path.

And, you know, the question becomes from some of the other school districts or some of the parents there at Providence, like, wait a minute, these folks have a math teacher in person. How come we don't? Well, it's because, A, it's the law of supply. There's not a lot of them coming out.

There's not a lot of math teachers being produced. And then, B, there's the law of demand. So if you need some math teachers, you've got to pay the market rate or more. And that market rate is above what we're paying. So, yes, my answer to that to you is, yes, I think, I mean, it's like a half a percent off, and most of it's cost of living.

So I think it's particularly appropriate for it to be 5%. It's a shame it could not be more because of this very, what's depicted here in this very slide. And I know that Dr. Murray struggles to get people here. So how do you get people?

You pay them a little bit more if you can. And so I think it's perfectly appropriate. Thank you, Mr. Baker. Yeah, so I'm not opposed to the 5%. I do support the 5%, just to be clear. I just want to address that because it was something that came up on, you know, our meeting last night, and you were present for us.

So I do appreciate the rebuttal, if you will, to the 3.7% comment versus the 5% and the backing from CBAC for that is also greatly appreciated. So I do appreciate that explanation. Yes, sir. 26 nieces and nephews.

That number right there is why. They are going to go through four years of college, take on four years of debt, and then be expected to go out into the world and make that much money, buy a house, buy a car, raise a family with a 3%, 5% raise every year when the cost of health insurance goes up even more than that.

That's why our kids in this generation are not choosing to go into the education field, and we need to do something to incentivize them. That's just my personal advantage. Thank you. I greatly appreciate that feedback. Thank you, guys.
Thank you. Thank you so much. Next, we have a 2026 legislative program update from Mr. Smith.

Thank you, Madam Chair, board members, for the opportunity to give you an update in the journalism session. I would note that we're not even quite halfway through the session, although it feels like we are. So a lot of work is being done.

I'm going to give some top-level updates this afternoon. I'm certainly happy to answer questions along the way. Obviously, our advocacy work continues at the General Assembly. The General Assembly had a little bit of a slower start than usual, mainly because you have the governor's inauguration, their staff getting in place, and certainly a brand-new General Assembly, both the House and Senate.

But the work has begun in earnest. In fact, next week is officially the halfway point. So we're looking forward to, obviously, to having additional updates along the way. I've left up on the slide deck here our legislative principles. As I talk about some of these updates, I just want to align those, obviously, with our principles along the way.

As you know, I've shared, obviously, with our board and our senior staff and other staff at legislative tracking sheet that I have, which tracks almost 300 pieces of legislation. I try to update that at least for the board once a week as I'm able to.

I think that's an important way for us to track legislation, provides mean opportunity to receive feedback from senior staff along the way of things that are of concern to them. It also helps us to keep perspective on things that we're hearing out there from different advocacy organizations, of things that may be of concern to us that we may not be tracking along the way.

The first thing I would note, obviously, is the status of the state budget. Officially, the legislative committees, money committees, will provide their updates on February 22nd. So we still have a little ways to go on that point. I will note, however, that both the House and Senate have passed what's known as House Bill 29, which is essentially this current fiscal year and updates that are with that.

From a political perspective, they have loaded up that budget bill with a lot of information regarding redistricting at the congressional level. There are actually a few budget updates embedded in that. One is with regards to the piece that Governor Youngkin put in place, which was a bonus there for 2% of our SOQ employees.

The General Assembly has shifted that focus to a $1,500 bonus. I would note that as we look at that, we're trying to work closely at some of the language that's embedded with the flexibility that's there to determine, in fact, if we do have some flexibility.

I've had some outreach to some of the money committee staffs this afternoon to get some additional information. They have shared that is their intent to write us flexibility. I've kind of noted that respectfully that the language does not suggest that. So they're looking at that in order to determine that piece.

And certainly, as you know, when we receive money from the General Assembly for bonuses as well as pay raises, again, that's only a portion of the cost. So they provide to us the state share of the SOQ positions. We have to come up with a local match for that.

And then we have the secondary conversation about all of our other employees and what they can be provided as well. And that, obviously, is the intent from the locality then to provide the rest of those funds. The bonus piece, obviously, has a concern for our employees because it's not embedded, obviously, in your salary piece.

But certainly, we are appreciative of the money that's been brought forward. But certainly, there's some additional analysis to be provided with that, which I will share as well as Mr. Meister as well. Legislatively, one of the big conversation points has been regarding legislation that passed last session regarding state assessments and tying assessments directly to SOL scores.

The General Assembly is still working through a couple different bills on that front. They still are very intent on tying that to SOLs, but there has been a little bit of movement on that front. That's sort of going to be something that's going to kind of progress over the next month or so, and I'll keep you updated with that.

You're all aware of legislation that's been discussed regarding having a portion of sales tax directed to school construction. In years past, the legislation has passed the General Assembly, only to be vetoed by then the governor. The current governor has indicated that she will, in fact, sign that legislation.

We're tracking that. Obviously, we understand there's pieces that come from that. It requires an affirmation by the local board supervisors, as well as a referendum by the voters. So that's something, obviously, that we know would have an impact in our school division, but it does not come directly to this governing body to make the first decision.

So we'll continue to work with that. Another piece that's come up for conversation is collective bargaining. The General Assembly has made it clear that they are going to shift the way the collective bargaining is done. That's something that we're going to closely watch to see the impacts we would have in our school division.

There's a couple of technicalities that kind of come with that. Certainly the definition of who can bargain as a particular unit, whether it's designed by affirmation of a job group or whether it's designed by sheer numbers of people. So we're looking closely at that, and certainly the impact there would be currently the process has to go from the school board to the board of supervisors to begin the collective bargaining process and coming back to the school division.

This change would shift to come directly to this governing body. The concern, obviously, that most school boards have is that you're bargaining without being able to raise revenue. And so certainly that's something just to be aware of. That is tracking, and I have said, I think, as a school division, we need to be prepared that that will change very quickly.

There's a delayed effective date to which the legislation would take in effect. However, people will begin to organize as of July 1 if this legislation passes. More to come with that. I mentioned in the budget piece for House Bill 29, they've embedded a lot of language regarding congressional redistricting.

The politics of that doesn't impact your work or my work. However, they are looking, some of this is tied from the court system, that it will require voting to take place on April 21st. As we're well aware, we're limited on the number of school instructional days that we have remaining that we need to adhere to.

There's a concern from school districts what would happen on April 21st. I would note we did have a little bit of a special election take place in early January. It only impacted about 19 of our schools. Congressional redistricting would impact all of our schools that serve as voting precincts.

So think in terms of more than 40-some schools will be impacted by that, and there certainly would be an aggressive push to push voters out at that time to come to the polls. Big picture, a couple of things just topic-wise to keep in mind, tracking conversations regarding paid sick leave, paid family and medical leave, and certainly some mandates along the way.

The General Assembly continues to grapple with conversations regarding serving student needs at the schools, knowing that we certainly, being in the large school divisions, have students with very many different needs, certainly around the medical perspective, and the General Assembly trying to put in place, whether it's diabetes care or other things, requirements upon our nurses, essentially.

And so I think we're trying to have the balance between being clear that we want to serve the needs of our students, but also understanding, certainly with our nurses, that they are overseeing hundreds, if not thousands, of students and trying to manage the day-to-day perspective that's put upon them as well.

With that, it's kind of a very general update, but I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have. Thank you, Mr. Smith. Board members, is there any discussion? Mr. Paranto. Thank you, Madam Chair.

I'll go on the third year now. We just need to build you a road to go straight to Richmond and back again. The amount of time that you spent up there advocating, we greatly appreciate that. What this one, this piece of legislation is driving towards a longer-term goal for the state of Virginia's average teacher salary to be commensurate with the average teacher salary across the nation.

As of today, we're about $7,000 to $8,000 below, so you can imagine that's going to take some time for us as a state to reach that goal should that be ultimately the stated goal at Richmond's level. I say this here to the extent that the General Assembly and the governor advance something greater than a 2% pay raise this year will probably be in service to achieving this longer-term goal. We're going to continue to wait and see. We need to see what the budget amendments actually look like. A smaller one, but I think an important one, as I think it's

Equity and at-risk funding. This was a big push at the end of last year's budget to add in some additional funding for these various groups.
